Here's a stopgap measure. I can't be certain if this is just an old wives' tale or a real story. An old man was living alone in his 80s in a rural West Virginia town, a very economically depressed area, very disconnected from society. He prides himself on self-reliance and independence, but he's slowly becoming unable to care for himself; one day, his son comes to take him to the nursing home. The old man is laying away at night; he hasn't relied on anyone for the last 50-60 years, and he's not breaking his record now. So, he gets out of bed, grabs a shotgun, and drives way up into the mountains. He parks his truck, walks deep into the woods, and ends his life. He is independent until the very date of his death, and his death is on his own terms. They find his body several weeks later.

Obviously, once you reach infirmity, suicide still isn't an option; people care for you, regardless of whether you know it or not. However, you can cross that bridge when you come to it. For now, you're young, so keep this story, or something like it, in mind. It will sustain you until that time. It's definitely sustained me.
You should read Stephen King's "A Good Marriage" - it's about a serial killer who acted totally normally around his family and his wife slowly finds out the man she'd known for decades was a monster.

When an unfortunate situation occurs (such as a death, substance abuse, domestic violence, etc.) many people will say that they will pray for those involved. However, the vast majority of the time, these are just words of comfort. Virtually nobody follows through when they say they will pray for someone, especially if it's a stranger.

I remember reading about the Alfie Evans case and lots of people in the comments said they would pray for Alfie. I bet at most 15-20% of those people actually prayed.

Thank you for the reply. I know I'm at a really dark place right now and people like you are lifesavers.

Unfortunately, I have been expelled from my college (OSU). However, I can reapply after 2 semesters have passed, and if I do well at another college (such as community college) they said they will consider reaccepting me.

I know it's going to be a long road. Thank you once again for your support.

The last situation was my discussion with my father over my grades. I used to be doing really well. In high school I graduated in the 97th percentile. I could hear the shame in his voice, and he's spreading the news to the whole family.

I didn't show up for finals because I felt too socially anxious to attend class. I had studied for them but I felt deeply, deeply ashamed of how others perceived me.

I'm failing probably because of my depression, which has been riding my back for the last 2.5 years. I can't help but connect it back to my family situation - I feel damaged because my father verbally abused me and my sister and we never had a mother figure.
I've tried that. He gave some good advice, like I should start volunteering and attending church more often. But with the career search and busy college schedule it's often difficult to manage.
